Family Health

How to use a vaginal pessary medicine safely

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A vaginal pessary or suppository is a medicine placed inside the vagina; it is different from a reusable support pessary for prolapse. Products vary in how they dissolve or release medicine, how much is absorbed and how they are inserted. They are not all faster than oral medicine or intended to act throughout the body. Your own pack leaflet and clinician’s instructions take priority.

First identify the medicine and the route

Check the medicine name, strength, prescribed dose, timing, expiry date and the words indicating vaginal use. Do not swallow a vaginal product or interchange vaginal and rectal routes. Antifungal, hormone and other vaginal medicines have different purposes and precautions; similar appearance does not make them interchangeable.

Ask a pharmacist to demonstrate using the supplied instructions if anything is unclear. Tell the prescriber about pregnancy or possible pregnancy, allergies, other medicines and unexplained symptoms. Do not assume a medicine is suitable in pregnancy because it goes into the vagina. If helping someone else, obtain their consent, protect privacy and follow professional advice rather than forcing insertion.

Prepare hands, supplies and the external skin

Have the correct medicine, its leaflet and any specified applicator ready on a clean surface. A clean towel and an unscented pad or liner may be useful. Wash and dry your hands before handling the medicine, then open the wrapper when ready; avoid touching it to unclean surfaces.

If washing is needed, gently clean the external vulval skin with warm water; mild unperfumed soap may be tolerated outside, but stop products that irritate. Do not put soap, cleansing fluid or water inside the vagina or douche. The vagina does not need internal washing before a dose; perfumed wipes, deodorants and repeated scrubbing can irritate.

Insert gently using the method for that product

Some products use a prefilled applicator, others need loading into one, and some are inserted with a clean finger. Follow the exact leaflet for assembly and loading. During pregnancy, certain products such as clotrimazole pessaries should be inserted without an applicator; this is not a rule to transfer to every vaginal medicine. Confirm your own instructions with the maternity team or pharmacist.

Choose the advised comfortable position, often lying with knees bent or standing with knees gently bent and feet apart. If an applicator is appropriate, guide it only as far as comfortably instructed; do not force it or aim for an arbitrary depth. Release the medicine as directed, usually by pressing the plunger to its stop, then withdraw the applicator. Stop and ask for help if insertion causes pain, resistance or bleeding.

After insertion and applicator care

Wash your hands afterwards. Dispose of wrappers and a single-use applicator as instructed, safely away from children; do not flush it. A disposable applicator must not be reused or shared. A medicine’s applicator design may differ from another pack, even for a similar treatment.

Only clean and reuse an applicator if its manufacturer explicitly permits this. Follow the specified disassembly, washing, rinsing, drying and storage steps. Do not invent a boiling, disinfectant or sterilizing method. If a device is damaged, incomplete or the directions are unclear, ask a pharmacist before the next dose.

Leakage, residue and bedtime use

Some leakage or residue is common with particular products, and a pad or liner may protect clothing. Bedtime may reduce leakage for some medicines, but prescribed timing and frequency still apply; not every dose can simply be moved to bedtime. Residue alone does not necessarily mean the treatment failed.

An intact tablet or large undissolved pieces coming out is different from expected residue. Ask a pharmacist whether the dose may have been ineffective; do not automatically insert another or double the next dose. A new offensive smell, worsening pain, bleeding or unusual discharge should not be dismissed as harmless medicine leakage.

Should a pessary be wetted before insertion?

There is no universal instruction to dip vaginal medicines in water. Use water only if the specific product leaflet or clinician says to. For example, the Fluomizin tablet instructions allow a drop of water for a very dry vagina; this does not authorize soaking other products or adding oil, soap or a lubricant.

If dryness makes insertion difficult or tablets repeatedly remain intact, ask for advice about the medicine and a suitable method. Do not force insertion, break or crush the dose, or add a vaginal moisturizer or another medicine without checking compatibility. Persistent dryness or pain may itself need assessment.

Storage and keeping the medicine intact

Read the labelled storage conditions and keep the medicine in its original packaging, away from children and pets. Protect it from unsuitable heat and moisture as directed. Refrigeration is not a general requirement: some products have a temperature limit, while others need no special storage conditions.

Do not freeze or refrigerate a product merely because it is called a suppository. Ask a pharmacist what to do if it has softened, crumbled, leaked from packaging or been stored incorrectly. Check expiry and packaging integrity; do not improvise repairs or combine broken fragments to guess a dose.

Periods, tampons and completing treatment

Whether to use a medicine during menstruation depends on the product. Current clotrimazole guidance says not to use pessaries during a period; Fluomizin instructions advise pausing and resuming afterwards. Other prescribed vaginal treatments may differ. If bleeding begins during a course, ask how to handle the schedule rather than following a blanket continue-or-stop rule.

Tampons may absorb medicine and reduce effectiveness; many vaginal treatments advise a pad or liner instead and prohibit other intravaginal products. Check instructions about menstrual cups, intercourse, condoms and diaphragms too: some medicines affect latex protection. Follow the prescribed course and any planned pauses; do not shorten, extend or repeat treatment or double a missed dose without the appropriate instructions.

When to get further help

Ask for advice if you cannot use the product comfortably, symptoms persist beyond its stated review point or keep returning, or you are unsure about a dose. New unexplained bleeding, sores, urinary pain or a changed discharge needs clinical assessment rather than another assumed thrush treatment. Fever, chills or worsening pelvic pain warrants prompt same-day advice; severe pelvic or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible.

Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or collapse after a medicine can be a serious allergic reaction: get immediate emergency help and do not take another dose while awaiting urgent advice. Do not wait for the course to finish. Bring the pack or a list of medicines when seeking help; careful technique cannot guarantee painless use or exclude another cause of symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current NHS and manufacturer instructions show that periods, pregnancy applicators, residue, wetting and storage depend on the medicine. The older MedlinePlus general technique page is useful for handling, but its generic menstrual advice does not override a current product leaflet.

Vaginal products include different local and hormone treatments; their absorption and devices vary. Product information does not support calling every vaginal medicine a rapidly absorbed systemic treatment or faster than oral therapy.

NHS external-hygiene advice excludes internal washing. Manufacturer warnings and NHS emergency allergy guidance support review of persistent or worsening symptoms and immediate emergency assessment for severe reactions.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record the medicine name, dose schedule, questions and symptoms for a pharmacist or clinician. It cannot identify an unknown product, choose a vaginal treatment or applicator, change pregnancy instructions or replace urgent care.

When to seek help

Use the prescribed route and exact leaflet. Do not swallow vaginal medicines, wash inside the vagina, force insertion, routinely wet or refrigerate products, reuse disposable devices or automatically repeat an expelled dose. Seek prompt same-day advice for fever or worsening pelvic pain; severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care. Sudden mouth or throat swelling or breathing or swallowing difficulty needs immediate emergency help. Confirm pregnancy and menstrual instructions with the care team.

Sources and further reading

  • UK National Health Service (NHS) — Clotrimazole: current pessary instructions, periods, leakage, tampons and follow-up
  • Bayer, UK product information on emc — Canesten 500mg Pessary: pregnancy without applicator, menstrual restrictions, handling and storage
  • Bayer, UK patient leaflet on emc — Canesten 100mg Pessary: reusable applicator instructions, residue and adverse reactions
  • Gedeon Richter, UK product information on emc — Fluomizin: product-specific moistening, menstrual pause, local action and storage
  • UK National Health Service (NHS) — Vaginal discharge: external hygiene, no internal washing and assessment of changed symptoms
  • US National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus — Vaginal progesterone: individual product directions and single-use applicators
  • US National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus — Vaginal estrogen: different preparations and individual instructions
  • UK National Health Service (NHS) — Anaphylaxis: emergency signs including airway swelling, breathing difficulty and collapse

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Read the instructions for the exact medicine, route and applicator; vaginal products are not interchangeable.
  • Wash hands and clean only the external skin as needed; never wash or soap inside the vagina.
  • Insert gently without forcing; pregnancy may change the applicator method for a particular product.
  • Leakage, wetting, storage, period use and applicator reuse all depend on the product; do not automatically redose.
  • Persistent symptoms need review; severe pain, heavy bleeding, collapse or signs of a serious allergy need immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

Is leakage after a vaginal pessary normal?

Some residue or leakage is expected with certain products and a liner may help. Follow the medicine’s timing instructions. An intact tablet or large undissolved pieces, worsening symptoms, offensive discharge or bleeding needs advice; do not automatically use another dose.

Can I wet a pessary to make insertion easier?

Only when its own instructions permit it. Some tablets have a specific water instruction for marked dryness, while others do not. Do not routinely soak medicines or add oil, soap or another product; ask if dryness or pain makes use difficult.

How do I stop the medicine breaking or melting before use?

Follow the storage label and keep the original packaging intact. Refrigeration is not suitable or necessary for every product. Ask a pharmacist about a damaged or incorrectly stored dose rather than crushing it, repairing it or guessing a replacement amount.

Can I use a vaginal pessary during my period?

It depends on the medicine. Some current product instructions say to avoid use during menstruation or pause and resume; other treatments differ. Ask about your exact course if bleeding starts. Do not use an older generic instruction as permission for every product.

Can I use a tampon at the same time?

Many vaginal medicines say not to, because tampons can absorb medicine; a pad or liner may be recommended. Check guidance for cups and other intravaginal products too, and whether the medicine affects condoms or diaphragms. Follow the product-specific advice.

Does every vaginal medicine need an applicator?

No. Some use a supplied applicator, some a prefilled device and some a clean finger. Pregnancy changes instructions for certain products, including clotrimazole. Ask rather than changing the device or applying one medicine’s method to another.

Should I wash inside my vagina first?

No. Wash and dry your hands, and gently clean the external vulval skin if needed. Do not douche or put soap or cleansing water inside the vagina. Follow applicator-cleaning instructions separately; cleaning a device does not mean washing inside your body.

When should I seek urgent help?

Fever, chills or worsening pelvic pain needs prompt same-day advice. Severe pelvic or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care, especially with possible pregnancy. Sudden airway or mouth swelling, trouble breathing or swallowing, or collapse after medicine also needs immediate emergency help; do not wait for another dose or completion of the course.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
